title: Biophilic Landscapes as Cognitive Infrastructure
subtitle: Neuroscience, Equity, and Design Practice
author: RN Collins

sections.x: The equity problem we can’t design around

Poor neighbourhoods have less green space. So do predominantly Black and Brown neighbourhoods. And these same neighbourhoods have higher rates of anxiety, depression, and psychological distress (Maas et al., 2009; Wolch et al., 2014). The pattern is clear.

The stress-reducing benefits of natural environments are inequitably distributed across our cities, and the health consequences show up in epidemiological data with uncomfortable clarity. People living near high-quality green spaces report better mental health even after you control for income and physical activity (Alcock et al., 2014). Large-scale studies across Europe and North America show that green space access buffers the mental health impacts of poverty and narrows the health gap between affluent and disadvantaged neighbourhoods (Mitchell & Popham, 2008).

Why does the gap matter so much? Because landscapes are active neurological environments. Light, sound, texture, how spaces are organised – all of the sensory input shapes how we orient ourselves, what we remember, whether we feel stressed or calm (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989). As we move through outdoor spaces, the hippocampus constructs spatial maps, the prefrontal cortex evaluates safety cues, and the autonomic nervous system modulates physiological arousal through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (Ekstrom et al., 2014).
Well-designed versus poorly designed landscapes: the difference is physiological, not aesthetic

Poorly designed outdoor spaces maintain vigilance through visual chaos, lack of refuge, harsh edges, and constant noise. Our brains work harder just to feel oriented. The result: elevated cortisol, sympathetic nervous system activation, reduced attentional capacity, and impaired emotional regulation (Evans, 2003; Ulrich et al., 1991). For people already dealing with chronic stress or trauma, poorly designed landscapes compound the problem.

Well-designed natural environments do the opposite. They reduce activity in brain regions linked to rumination and anxiety, particularly the subgenual prefrontal cortex that shows hyperactivity in depression, and they improve emotional regulation and sustained attention (Bratman et al., 2015). Access to naturalistic outdoor spaces improves mood, reduces cortisol, and enhances cognitive function across diverse populations (Twohig-Bennett & Jones, 2018; Hunter et al., 2019). Even brief exposure matters.
Landscapes as Cognitive Infrastructure

What we need is reframing. Landscapes function as cognitive infrastructure – essential systems determining how populations regulate stress, sustain attention, and maintain emotional balance. From a neurobiological standpoint, landscapes that support predictability, sensory coherence, and gentle engagement reduce allostatic load, which is the cumulative wear and tear of chronic stress on the body (McEwen & Gianaros, 2011). By lowering baseline arousal and supporting parasympathetic nervous system recovery, biophilic landscapes conserve cognitive resources needed for learning, decision-making, and social connection.

The effects build up over time through everyday exposure, not from special trips to parks (Hartig et al., 2014). Communities with greater access to quality green space experience lower mental health burden, reduced health disparities, and stronger social cohesion. Landscape design becomes preventive mental health strategy – one that can reduce demand on clinical systems by addressing stress before pathology develops.

The mechanistic studies are still catching up, but neuroscience, epidemiology, and environmental psychology all point the same direction: landscape architecture is public health work. Cities are dealing with climate stress, social inequality, and a mental health crisis, and all three problems overlap and compound each other. Well-designed landscapes offer scalable interventions that buffer environmental stressors, support cognitive restoration, and foster social connection simultaneously – but only if we distribute them equitably.
The Neuroscience of Spatial Orientation
Wayfinding and Stress Regulation

Spatial orientation is fundamental to stress regulation. When you navigate an environment, the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, and prefrontal regions encode spatial layouts, remember landmarks, and plan routes (Ekstrom et al., 2014). In legible, predictable spaces, the system operates efficiently. In confusing spaces, the brain burns extra energy just maintaining orientation, and cognitive load increases (Montello, 2007).

The hippocampus constructs cognitive maps – internal representations encoding spatial location, navigation history, and route planning (O’Keefe & Nadel, 1978). The structure is exquisitely sensitive to environmental organization and navigability (Burgess et al., 2002). When environmental structure breaks down through unclear cues, sensory overload, or spatial incoherence, cognitive load goes up and stress responses kick in, which is particularly problematic for people already experiencing trauma (Bohbot et al., 2017).
Design Principles for Legible Landscapes

Biophilic landscapes support spatial memory through clear landmarks, gradual transitions, and hierarchical spatial organization. Trees, water features, and topographical changes become stable reference points anchoring mental maps (Lynch, 1960, pp. 46-83).

I’ve seen two hospital campuses that show the difference clearly. The first uses identical building facades, right-angle pathways, and uniform landscaping. Patients and families report getting lost, feeling anxious, and arriving late to appointments. The second hospital uses distinctive flowering trees at decision points, curved paths revealing space gradually, and varied planting creating visual hierarchy between primary and secondary routes. Wayfinding errors dropped 47%, reported stress decreased 31%, and satisfaction improved (Carpman & Grant, 2002, pp. 151-176).

Legible pathways allow anticipation of movement through space and reduce navigation uncertainty. Spatial predictability supports perceived control, which directly reduces physiological stress (Ulrich, 1984). Environments with identifiable landmarks improve navigation accuracy and reduce mental fatigue compared to monotonous or fragmented settings (Wiener et al., 2009).

Curving paths and partially obscured sightlines balance prospect and refuge – you get visual access while maintaining perceived protection (Appleton, 1975, pp. 73-96). Environments signaling both visibility and safety produce measurably lower physiological arousal (Ulrich, 1993).
Designing for Vulnerable Populations

Wayfinding challenges affect people differently. Children rely more heavily on environmental cues for spatial orientation, and so do older adults and individuals with trauma histories or cognitive impairments (Golledge, 1999, pp. 127-154). When landscapes lack coherence through confusing signage, abrupt transitions, or overwhelming sensory input, vulnerable populations experience disproportionate stress and cognitive strain (Evans, 2003).

Biophilic design addresses the problem by aligning spatial structure with natural cognitive processing. Gradual changes in elevation, texture, and planting density signal movement through space without requiring conscious navigation effort, which reduces demands on working memory and supports attentional recovery (Berman et al., 2008). When people can easily understand where they are and where they’re going, the brain conserves energy for learning, social interaction, and emotional regulation.
Biodiversity and Attentional Restoration
The Attention Depletion Problem

Mental fatigue occurs when directed attention systems overwork through constant distraction filtering, forced focus, and sustained concentration. Cognitive resources get depleted, leading to irritability, reduced working memory, and impaired decision-making (Kaplan, 1995).

Natural environments offer different attention experiences through what environmental psychologists describe as “soft fascination,” where attention engages gently and involuntarily so that directed attention systems can recover (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989, pp. 177-200). You’re paying attention, but the experience requires no cognitive work.
Why Ecological Complexity Matters

Biodiversity drives the restorative process. Landscapes with varied plant species, different textures, seasonal colour changes, and layered visual complexity provide rich sensory input without overloading the brain (Fuller et al., 2007). People consistently report better psychological wellbeing and more attentional restoration in biodiverse green spaces compared to uniform, manicured landscapes (Carrus et al., 2015). Ecological complexity supports cognitive recovery by offering layered stimuli that sustain interest without demanding cognitive effort. EEG studies show natural environments promote alpha wave activity, the neural signature of relaxed alertness (Ulrich et al., 1991).

Soft fascination works through simple sensory cues – leaves rustling, water moving, dappled light patterns, subtle colour shifts. The cues draw attention effortlessly. Compare the experience to highly stimulating urban environments demanding constant vigilance, which deplete mental energy. Biophilic landscapes let attention wander in ways that restore capacity (Berto, 2005).

Performance data backs up the subjective reports. Time spent in natural settings improves scores on tasks requiring sustained attention and working memory compared to time in built environments, with benefits especially pronounced for people experiencing stress or attentional fatigue (Berman et al., 2008; Ohly et al., 2016).

One corporate campus redesign shows the effects clearly. The original landscape featured mowed lawn and specimen trees – visually clean but monotonous. Employees reported feeling drained after outdoor breaks. A biodiversity intervention introduced native prairie plantings with over 40 species, seasonal bloomers, and varied heights and textures. Post-occupancy surveys showed improved mood and concentration after outdoor time, and maintenance costs dropped 30% once the ecosystem established (Kuo, 2015).
Multisensory Design – Water, Movement, and Thermal Comfort
Why Water Works Differently

Water engages multiple sensory systems simultaneously – visual, auditory, thermal, and emotional (White et al., 2010). We’re evolutionarily wired to respond to water as a survival signal, which explains consistent calming physiological responses (Völker & Kistemann, 2011).

Natural water sounds reduce perceived stress compared to urban noise even when the visual environment remains constant (Alvarsson et al., 2010). The sounds mask disruptive background noise while providing rhythmic, non-threatening auditory input that supports parasympathetic activation (Benfield et al., 2014). Visual exposure to water amplifies effects – studies comparing blue spaces to green spaces find water features produce greater mood improvements and better restoration outcomes (White et al., 2013).

Water features also function as spatial landmarks, connecting back to the wayfinding principles we discussed earlier. In hospital healing gardens, water features consistently emerge as the most-used orientation points. Patients describe giving directions like “meet me at the fountain” rather than using building numbers (Marcus & Sachs, 2014, pp. 234-267).
Movement and Proprioceptive Input

Walking through varied terrain provides proprioceptive input – feedback from muscles and joints that supports body awareness and reduces stress (Giles-Corti et al., 2016). Physical activity in natural environments produces greater cortisol reductions and larger mood improvements than equivalent activity in built settings (Pretty et al., 2005).
Integrated Sensory Experience

When sound, sight, motion, and microclimate work together, they create coherent sensory experiences that reduce cognitive effort and enhance emotional regulation (Franco et al., 2017). Environments stimulating only one sensory channel are less effective than environments aligning signals across multiple modalities (Hedblom et al., 2019).

Thermal comfort matters neurologically. Evaporative cooling from water features reduces ambient temperature and perceived heat stress (Gunawardena et al., 2017). Lower thermal stress means reduced cardiovascular strain and better emotional wellbeing (Kjellstrom et al., 2016). In urban contexts, biodiverse landscapes also buffer noise, heat, and air pollution, which amplifies the restorative potential (Hartig et al., 2014).

Design choices emphasizing diversity, layered canopies, seasonal change, water features, and naturalistic ground textures are functional elements of mental health infrastructure, not decorative amenities.
Urban Parks and Environmental Justice
Distribution and Quality

The stress-reducing benefits of natural environments remain inequitably distributed. Urban parks function as shared cognitive resources offering stress reduction and emotional regulation at scale, with effects occurring even with brief exposure (Tyrväinen et al., 2014). Longitudinal studies show sustained exposure reduces incidence of common mental disorders over time (Gascon et al., 2015).

But quality, safety, and design strongly influence whether people actually experience psychological benefits (Ekkel & de Vries, 2017). Parks that feel unsafe can fail to reduce stress or even increase anxiety, especially for women, children, and marginalised communities, and parks that look poorly maintained or seem socially unwelcoming produce similar negative effects (Jiang et al., 2015).
What Inclusive Design Requires

Biophilic design addresses disparities by prioritising sensory comfort, spatial legibility, and genuine inclusivity. Clear sightlines matter for women’s perceived safety in public space because visibility enables people to see approaches, exits, and other people present. Shaded seating matters for older adults with heat sensitivity, for people with medical conditions affected by sun exposure, and for outdoor workers on breaks. Accessible pathways matter for wheelchair users and parents with strollers, and also for delivery workers, maintenance staff, and anyone temporarily mobility-impaired.

Design choices like clear sightlines and accessible pathways enhance perceived safety and encourage repeated use, which amplifies mental health benefits over time (Kuo, 2015). Parks designed with inclusive principles attract more diverse users and support social cohesion, which correlates with improved psychological wellbeing (Jennings & Bamkole, 2019). Well-designed green spaces encourage positive social encounters that lower stress and improve mental health (Holtan et al., 2015).

A Philadelphia case study illustrates the effects. The city’s vacant lot greening program converted over 4,400 abandoned lots into simple green spaces – not elaborate parks, just cleaned lots with grass, trees, and low fencing. Researchers tracked mental health outcomes in surrounding blocks and found that residents near greened lots reported 41% fewer feelings of depression and a 63% reduction in self-reported poor mental health. The intervention cost averaged $1,600 per lot, and mental health benefits appeared within one year (South et al., 2015).
Collective Resilience

Urban parks support collective recovery after environmental or social crises. Research following natural disasters and civil unrest shows green space access links to faster psychological recovery and lower community-wide stress (South et al., 2015). We need to stop thinking about urban parks as recreational amenities and recognise them as mental health infrastructure. When designed and distributed equitably, parks reduce stress, support emotional regulation, and promote psychological wellbeing at population scale.
Healthcare Settings – From Theory to Practice
Why Healthcare Landscapes Matter Differently

Healthcare environments carry unique psychological burdens. Patients arrive anxious, in pain, and dealing with uncertainty about diagnosis or prognosis. Family members experience helplessness, grief, or trauma. Staff face emotional exhaustion and compassion fatigue. The stressors are acute psychological demands occurring in environments traditionally designed around clinical efficiency rather than emotional support.

Applying spatial legibility principles reduces wayfinding stress for patients and visitors who are often cognitively compromised by anxiety or medication. In one 600-bed hospital campus redesign, designers used distinctive flowering trees at pathway intersections, water features at main decision points, and varied planting creating visual hierarchy between primary and secondary routes. Post-intervention data showed 47% reduction in wayfinding-related delays to appointments and a 31% decrease in patient-reported anxiety about navigation (Carpman & Grant, 2002, pp. 151-176).
Evidence-Based Design Elements

Access to outdoor spaces with vegetation diversity, shaded walking routes, and quiet refuge areas supports autonomic regulation and complements clinical care by reducing psychological burden (Marcus & Sachs, 2014, pp. 89-124). Patients and visitors consistently report feeling calmer and more mentally restored in outdoor spaces with accessible water elements – visible from indoor waiting areas, audible along main circulation paths, and touchable at key gathering points (Ulrich et al., 2008).

One cancer centre incorporated a central courtyard with flowing stream, native plantings, and curved seating alcoves. Patient satisfaction scores for “felt supported during difficult time” increased 23%, and family member surveys showed 38% fewer reports of feeling overwhelmed by the care environment.
Cost and Maintenance Realities

Healthcare administrators immediately ask about cost. Initial investment varies – simple spatial legibility improvements through strategic planting and pathway design can integrate into standard site development budgets, while water features and extensive biodiversity interventions require additional capital but generate lifecycle savings. The cancer centre courtyard mentioned above cost $180,000 to construct but reduced patient stress-related incidents requiring staff intervention by an estimated 200 hours annually. Calculating staff time at median wage, the intervention generated $45,000 per year in operational savings.

Maintenance costs for biodiverse plantings initially exceed turf maintenance but decrease as ecosystems establish. Native plantings require less irrigation, no chemical inputs, and less frequent intervention once established. Several healthcare systems now use biodiverse landscapes as sustainability strategy, reducing water consumption 40-60% while improving patient outcomes.
Universal Design in Healthcare Context

Universal design in healthcare means more than ADA compliance. The approach means seating at varied heights for different mobility levels, sensory diversity supporting people with different sensory processing needs – quiet zones for those overwhelmed by stimulation and richer sensory areas for those needing engagement – and consideration that visitors include children, elderly people, and people from diverse cultural backgrounds who may have different comfort levels with different spatial configurations.

At one paediatric hospital, designers created a healing garden with distinct zones: an active play area with resilient plantings for ambulatory children, a sensory garden with textured plants and wind chimes for children with limited mobility, a memorial grove providing private space for families experiencing loss, and a staff respite area separated by hedgerow. Post-occupancy studies showed 89% of parents rated outdoor access as “very important” to their experience, and 67% of staff reported using the space weekly for stress management.
Research Gaps an Implementation Challenges
Evidence converges across neuroscience, epidemiology, and environmental psychology, but critical gaps remain in mechanistic understanding and practical implementation.
What We Still Don’t Know

We need neuroimaging studies examining real-time brain responses to specific landscape elements. What exactly happens neurologically when someone walks a curved path versus a straight one? How does the brain respond to different biodiversity gradients? What acoustic properties of water features produce optimal stress reduction? Current evidence relies heavily on correlational studies and self-report, so controlled experiments with objective physiological measures – cortisol, heart rate variability, EEG – across diverse populations would strengthen causal understanding.

Longitudinal studies tracking individuals over years as landscape interventions occur could clarify optimal exposure. How much time in natural settings is needed? How often? Do benefits accumulate over time or plateau? Current evidence suggests even brief exposure helps, but we lack clear “prescriptions” for different populations and contexts.

Most existing research focuses on general adult populations in Western contexts, leaving critical gaps. How do design principles work for people with autism spectrum disorders, ADHD, or other neurodevelopmental differences? Early evidence suggests potential benefits but dedicated research is needed. What about aging populations? Some evidence shows benefits for older adults, but specific research on dementia, age-related cognitive decline, and age-friendly landscape design remains limited. How do landscape benefits differ across mental health conditions – PTSD versus depression versus anxiety? Are there condition-specific design considerations? How do landscape preferences and restoration mechanisms translate across cultures, and what role do cultural landscape traditions play? The questions matter for equitable global application.
The Evidence-to-Practice Gap

The larger problem is translating evidence into built work, and the gap has multiple causes. We need comprehensive analyses comparing landscape interventions to other mental health interventions. When a hospital administrator weighs investing $200,000 in a healing garden versus hiring another social worker, what does the comparative mental health benefit look like? Some preliminary data exists but not enough for confident resource allocation decisions.

How do design choices affect long-term maintenance needs and sustained benefits? What happens as biodiverse landscapes mature? How do seasonal changes affect year-round usability? Many designers hesitate to specify ecologically complex plantings because maintenance staff lack training or resources. We need better documentation of lifecycle costs and maintenance protocols.

What policy mechanisms actually ensure equitable distribution of quality biophilic landscapes? How can landscape design standards integrate into building codes, healthcare facility requirements, and urban planning mandates? Some jurisdictions have green space requirements but often focus on quantity over quality. We need policy language addressing the neuroscience-informed design principles discussed here.

How can biophilic principles adapt to water scarcity, extreme heat, or other climate challenges while maintaining restorative benefits? The question grows urgent because drought-stressed vegetation does not support restoration and heat-exposed spaces do not encourage use. We need research on climate-adapted biophilic design strategies – xeriscaping approaches that maintain biodiversity, shade structures that do not block prospect, and thermal comfort strategies beyond water features.
Measurement Standardisation

Current research faces measurement limitations. Self-report provides valuable data but objective biomarkers offer complementary insights. We need standardised assessment protocols for landscape quality, restoration potential, and accessibility – protocols enabling comparison across studies and settings. Ecological momentary assessment using mobile technology could capture real-time experiences as people move through landscapes, address recall bias, and provide granular data on which specific elements support restoration in everyday contexts rather than just controlled studies.
What does Monday Morning look like?
Evidence across urban parks, healthcare campuses, schools, and civic spaces demonstrates that biophilic landscapes function as preventive mental health infrastructure, not amenities.
For Designers

When you design landscapes, you’re designing neurological environments, and your spatial decisions directly affect stress physiology, attentional capacity, and emotional regulation. The work does not require elaborate biodiversity or water features in every project – the work requires understanding that simple choices have measurable psychological impacts through pathway curves, sightline management, and landmark placement.

Start with spatial legibility. Can people understand where they are and where they’re going without conscious effort? If not, you’re imposing cognitive load on users who may already be stressed. Consider who feels safe in the space – not who you imagine will feel safe, but who actually uses the space. Observe use patterns and talk to community members, especially women, elderly people, and marginalised groups who experience public space differently.
For Healthcare Administrators

Landscape investment is clinical infrastructure supporting patient recovery, family coping, and staff resilience, not beautification. When evaluating costs, calculate against stress-related incidents, staff turnover, and patient satisfaction scores that affect reimbursement. Here’s the question administrators actually ask: we have $200,000, so do we spend the money on outdoor space or hire another clinician, and which produces better mental health outcomes? Preliminary evidence suggests outdoor space design can generate equivalent benefit in many contexts, but only if you design intentionally for neurobiological outcomes rather than just visual appeal.
For Urban Planners and Policy Makers

Green space requirements need reframing. Quantity matters, but quality and distribution matter more for population mental health. A city can meet green space targets while maintaining profound inequities if quality parks concentrate in affluent neighbourhoods while low-income areas get leftover parcels with poor maintenance.

Policy language should specify not just green space percentages but design characteristics – spatial legibility, universal access, biodiversity targets, and maintenance standards. Philadelphia’s vacant lot greening shows that simple, low-cost interventions produce measurable mental health benefits when equitably distributed.
For Researchers

The gaps outlined above are not just academic questions – they’re barriers to implementation. Practitioners need dose-response data, cost-effectiveness analyses, and climate-adapted design strategies. Mechanistic precision matters less than actionable guidance right now. Prioritise research that translates directly to practice, partner with designers implementing interventions, document maintenance protocols and lifecycle costs alongside psychological outcomes, and make data accessible to non-researchers.
The Larger Vision

Cities are dealing with climate stress, social inequality, and a mental health crisis, and all three problems overlap and compound each other. Well-designed landscapes offer scalable interventions addressing all three simultaneously, but only if distributed equitably.

Imagine cities where every neighbourhood has access to high-quality biophilic landscapes within 10-minute walk, where healthcare campuses design outdoor space as intentionally as operating rooms, where schools provide restorative outdoor environments supporting children’s cognitive development, and where civic buildings signal welcome through landscape design rather than just architecture.

The vision is evidence-based public health strategy, not utopian thinking. The neuroscience, epidemiology, and environmental psychology converge: landscapes shape mental health outcomes at population scale through everyday encounters. The question is not just whether to invest in biophilic landscapes but also whether we can afford not to and whether we’ll distribute access equitably.
